To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

neutrophil migration to alveolar spaces during streptococcemia occurs independently of selectin-mediated neutrophil-endothelial interactions and that selectins do not mediate neutrophil margina- tion within pulmonary capillari.

neutrophilic margination in pulmonary capillaries is independent of selectins, that the neutrophilia is not associated with increased marginations in noncapillaries, that the neutropenia is associated with decreased emigration of neutrophiils during pneumococcal pneumonia, and that neutrophil emigtration can occur despite the absence of all known selectins.
the pulmonary capillary endothelium is a barrier to the margination of neutro- philic WBC, and that this barrier is not due to the presence of E- or P-selectin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which the immune system recognizes and destroys invading microorganisms.
the mechanisms by which neutrophils traffic to sites of infection.
the mechanisms of pulmonary neutrophil marginaion and emigration in uninfected and infected mice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

E- and P- selectins are required for normal neutrophil marginaion in the pulmonary capillary bed, but not in the non-capillary microvessels; that E- and/or P-selectins are not required for neutrophil margnation in non-capillary vessels during streptococal pneumonia; and that emigration of neutrohilis into alveolar spaces during streptococcus pneumonia can occur despite deficiency/inhibition of E- and P selectins.
E- and P- selectins do not play a major role in the margination of neutraphils in pulmonary capillaries, but do play a role in the migration of neutrophills to alveoli in the lungs of mice.

the E- and P- selectin deficiency does not alter neutrophil marginations in pulmonary microvessles and that E- and P selectin deficiency does alter neutrophil emigrations during streptococcus pneumonia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
selectins are not required for neutrophil marginaion in the pulmonary circulation but may play a role in the emigration of neutophils to alveolar spaces.
selectins do not play an important role in neutrophil marginations and emigration in the murine lung.
E- and P- selectins are not required for neutrophil margnation within pulmonary capilleries but may be required for the emigration of these cells from alveoli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neutrophil emigrations in response to bacterial infections are not dependent upon selectin function.
E- and P- selectin deficiency does not affect the ability of neutrophils in the blood to migrate to sites of infection.
selectins do not play a significant role in neutrophil emigratiion in the lung.
